13.4 Solutions to Exercises 4 - Exercises on normal subgroups, simplicity and Lagrange’s Theorem Solution. (Question 4.4.1) We must show that for all h ∈ H and all k ∈ H ∩ N we have that h −1kh ∈ H ∩ N . Fix k ∈ H ∩ N and fix h ∈ H. Now h−1kh ∈ H because h, k ∈ H. Also h−1kh ∈ N because N is normal in G. Therefore h−1kh ∈ H ∩ N . Solution. (Question 4.4.2) Well ∣S5∣ = 5! = 5 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 23. By Lagrange, the order of any subgroup of S5 must divide the order of S5. Since 9 does not divide 5!, there is no subgroup of S5 of order 9. Solution. (Question 4.4.3) We first show that HN ⊆ N H. Fix hk ∈ HN , with h ∈ H and k ∈ N . Because N is normal, we can use the Order Switching Lemma, to deduce that there exists k′ ∈ N such that hk = k′h. But k′h ∈ N H. Hence HN ⊆ N H. To show N H ⊆ HN , we now reverse the above argument: Fix kh ∈ N H. Because N is normal, there exists k′′ ∈ N such that kh = hk′′. But hk′′ ∈ HN . Hence N H ⊆ HN . Solution. (Question 4.4.4) (a) Suppose H ≤ G. By Lagrange’s Theorem, ∣H∣ divides ∣G∣ = p. But p is prime, so ∣H∣ = 1 or p. In other words, ∣H∣ = 1 or ∣H∣ = ∣G∣. We know from a previous problem sheet that this implies that H = ⟨eG⟩ or H = G. (b) To show G is cyclic, we need to find some g ∈ G such that G = ⟨g⟩. Choose any nontrivial g ∈ G. We know ⟨g⟩ is a subgroup of G. Because g /= eG, we also know that ⟨g⟩ /= ⟨eG⟩. By part (a), the only subgroups of G are ⟨eG⟩ and G. Hence ⟨g⟩ = G. Solution. (Question 4.4.5) We just need to check the conditions of the Quick Subgroup Test: identity, closure, inverse. • [Identity] Now eG lies in H and N , and so eGeG ∈ HN . Hence, eG ∈ HN . • [Closure] Fix two elements in HN , by fixing h1, h2 ∈ H and k1, k2 ∈ N and considering h1k1 ∈ HN and h2k2 ∈ HN . Now we want to show (h1k1)(h2k2) lies in HN . For this we use the Order Switching Lemma to change the orders. Now (h1k1)(h2k2) = h1(k1h2)k2. We can apply the Order Switching Lemma to k1h2 to deduce there exists k′ 1 ∈ N such that k1h2 = h2k′ 1. Hence, (h1k1)(h2k2) = h1(k1h2)k2 = (h1h2)(k′ 1k2) ∈ HN. • [Inverse] Fix an element in HN , by fixing h ∈ H and k ∈ N and considering hk ∈ HN . Now (hk)−1 = k−1h−1. We must show that k−1h−1 ∈ HK. We can apply the Order Switching Lemma to deduce that there exists k′ ∈ N such that k−1h−1 = h −1k′. But h−1k′ ∈ HN , therefore (hk) −1 ∈ HN . Solution. (Question 4.4.6) Recall that S3 = {e, (123), (132), (12), (13), (23)} and C3 = {e, (123), (132)}. In S3, the product of a 2-cycle and a 3-cycle is always a 2-cycle (this is easily checked). Moreover, the product of two 2-cycles is either trivial (if the 2-cycles are equal) or it is a 3-cycle (again this is easily checked). Now we know this, we can check for normality. Fix g ∈ S3 and c ∈ C3. We must show that g−1cg ∈ C3. Note that either g ∈ C3, or g is a 2-cycle.

• If g ∈ C3, then g−1cg ∈ C3 (by closure property of C3.) • If g is a 2-cycle, then g−1 = g and so g−1 is also a 2-cycle. Hence g−1c is a 2-cycle. Therefore g−1cg = (g−1c)g is a product of two 2-cycles and is therefore either trivial or a 3-cycle. In both cases, it lies in C3. Hence, g−1cg ∈ C3, and so C3 ⊴ S3. Solution. (Question 4.4.7) (a) This permutation fixes every element in Z except 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10. Therefore it fixes all but finitely many elements of Z, so it lies in FS(Z). (b) This permutation fixes only 0, and every other element in Z is moved. Hence it does not lie in FS(Z). (c) Every element in FS(Z) is a permutation of Z, and therefore lies in Sym(Z). Hence FS(Z) ⊆ Sym(Z) and we can use the Quick Subgroup Test: [Identity] e fixes all but finitely many elements of Z (in fact it fixes all elements) and so e ∈ FS(Z) [Closure] If ρ, τ ∈ FS(Z), then they both move only finitely many things in Z. Hence their product moves only finitely many things. [Inverse] If ρ ∈ FS(Z) then ρ−1 is a permutation moving only finitely many things (since it must “undo” those things moved by τ ) and so it lies in FS(Z). (d) The group is not abelian, since any permutations in Sn can be thought of as lying in FS(Z) and we know there are elements in Sn that do not commute. (e) Suppose g ∈ Sym(Z) and h ∈ FS(Z). We must show that g−1hg ∈ FS(Z). Now let X ⊆ Z be the set of elements of Z that are not fixed by h. By definition of FS(Z), we know that X is finite. This set X is called the support of h. Now let g−1X = {g−1n ∶ n ∈ X} and notice that X and g−1X contain the same number of elements. Suppose m /∈ g−1X. Then gm /∈ X. We therefore have that hgm = gm (this is because X contains all the things that are moved by h). Therefore g−1hgm = g−1gm = m. In other words, g−1hg fixes everything that does not lie in g−1X. Since the set g−1X is finite, we therefore have that g−1hg only moves finitely many elements in Z, and therefore g−1hg ∈ FS(Z).
